sentences.text: Martharaptor is distinguished by skeletal features in the hands and feet that are intermediate between early therizinosauroids and advanced therizinosaurids.
The hand claws of this animal are distinctive, showing a height greater than their length along with strong curvature.
One preserved hand claw is larger and likely from the first finger, while the second and third finger claws are equal in size.
The fourth metatarsal is beveled, a feature intermediate between Falcarius and therizinosaurids.
The skull of Martharaptor is unknown.
The hand claws are so strong that their curved length from the tip to a right angle on the back surface is less than the height of that back surface.
The first metatarsal touches the top of the ankle without flattening, unlike most theropods.
The first toe presumably had no function, similar to later Therizinosauridae.
The holotype specimen UMNH VP 21400 was found at the Hayden-Corbett site, about eight miles southeast of Green River, Utah.
The genus name Martharaptor honors paleontologist assistant Martha C. Hayden, and the species name greenriverensis refers to the Green River.
The species Martharaptor greenriverensis was named and described in 2012 by Philip Senter, James Kirkland, and Deblieux Donald.
The find consisted of loose bones scattered over an area of one square meter at a depth of twenty centimeters.
Typical therizinosaur characteristics include strongly curved relatively narrow claws and the absence of hinge joints in the mid-foot bones.
Phylogenetic analysis places Martharaptor within Therizinosauroidea as the sister taxon to the Alxasaurus + Therizinosauridae group, though support is weak.
The describers placed Martharaptor within the group Therizinosauroidea.
Cladistic analysis placed Martharaptor in a basal position, above Beipiaosaurus but below Alxasaurus on the family tree.
Martharaptor lived during the Early Cretaceous in the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah.
Martharaptor greenriverensis lived in the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 124 million years ago during the Aptian stage in what is now North America.
The holotype specimen UMNH VP 21400 dates to the early Aptian, approximately 124 million years ago.
The genus lived during the Valanginian stage, between 137.05 and 132.6 million years ago.
The describers noted that the phylogenetic position was very uncertain due to the poor quality of the findings.
